Testimony establishes what the witness reported; it does not independently measure extraordinary performance or establish origin.

events.summary: Miguel Alcubierre described a mathematical spacetime geometry that permits a moving region of space without locally exceeding light speed. established: The original paper develops a mathematical metric and discusses negative energy requirements.

limitations: No laboratory vehicle, power source, control system or practical deployment is demonstrated.

events.title: Early Homo sapiens evidence at Jebel Irhoud
events.summary: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco combine facial and dental features associated with Homo sapiens with a more primitive braincase. Dating of heated flints from the associated archaeological layer yielded about 315,000 years, with substantial uncertainty. The 2017 studies expanded the geographic and chronological evidence available for reconstructing early human evolution across Africa.
events.significance: This evidence gives the chronology a deep African starting point and makes human origins a changing research problem rather than a single birthplace or sudden event.
established: Layer 7 thermoluminescence estimate: 315 ± 34 ka at 1σ.
The morphology paper describes a mosaic of modern-looking and more primitive features.
limitations: The dated material is associated heated flint; the estimate is not a direct calendar date for every fossil.
These finds do not identify the first Homo sapiens or establish one geographic origin for the species.

events.title: An ochre drawing at Blombos Cave
events.summary: A small silcrete flake from Blombos Cave in South Africa bears intersecting red lines that researchers identified as an intentionally applied ochre drawing. The flake came from layer CCC in the M1 phase, dated to about 73,000 years ago. Microscopic and chemical study supported a crayon-like application, while the design's meaning remains unknown.
events.significance: The object makes early graphic practice visible through material evidence, while leaving a clear boundary between identifying deliberate marks and interpreting what those marks meant.
established: The inspected Figure 1 labels M1 as 73 ± 3 ka using OSL dates.
The authors identify deliberately applied ochre lines on ground silcrete.
limitations: Context dating estimates the archaeological phase, not the exact moment of drawing.
The pattern does not establish language, a particular belief, or a decipherable symbolic message.

events.title: Aristotle argues for a single cosmos
events.summary: In On the Heavens, Aristotle organised the cosmos through arguments about natural bodies and their motions. He distinguished circular heavenly motion from terrestrial motions and argued that the universe contains all available matter, leaving no material for additional worlds. This entry records a philosophical model and its reasoning, rather than an observational demonstration of cosmic uniqueness.
events.significance: A chronology of knowledge includes durable frameworks that were later challenged; Aristotle's account makes the premises behind one influential picture of the heavens open to inspection.
established: Book I distinguishes circular and straight natural motions.
Book I, parts 8–9, argues that there is only one heaven or cosmos.
limitations: The surviving argument is historical natural philosophy, not evidence that only one planetary system exists.
The approximate date cannot be resolved to a precise year or day from the inspected text.

sources.locator: Book I, parts 2–3 and 8–9; host composition-date header
supports: The translated text sets out motion categories and argues that a cosmos containing all matter cannot have additional material worlds beyond it.

events.title: Epicurus reasons about innumerable worlds
events.summary: Epicurus's Letter to Herodotus argues that infinite atoms and space permit innumerable worlds, some similar to ours and some different. The argument belongs to an atomist account of nature preserved in the ancient textual tradition. It demonstrates that a plurality of worlds was thinkable long before instruments could establish the existence of planets around other stars.
events.significance: The letter distinguishes the history of possible worlds from their detection, giving readers a clear example of a speculative argument that predates observational tests.
established: The letter explicitly argues for infinitely many worlds, including worlds unlike ours.
Its stated basis is an argument about atoms and infinity, not telescopic evidence.
limitations: Ancient ‘worlds’ cannot be equated without qualification with modern exoplanets.
Neither a precise composition date nor evidence of extraterrestrial life follows from this passage.

sources.locator: Section 11 of the displayed letter, on infinite worlds
supports: The passage derives an unlimited number of worlds, both similar and dissimilar, from its preceding atomist premises.

contextLinks.note: The texts offer contrasting historical positions, without demonstrating direct transmission between them.
A comparison of different evidential activities: philosophical possibility versus a reported planetary detection. No causal lineage is claimed.

events.title: Aryabhata explains apparent stellar motion
events.summary: The Aryabhatiya combines mathematical rules with an account of astronomical cycles. In a famous comparison, a traveller in a moving boat sees stationary objects move backward, just as an observer sees stars move westward. The text supports an Earth-rotation interpretation, although adjacent verses and later commentaries complicate reconstruction of the author's complete cosmological system.
events.significance: This entry broadens the history of mathematical astronomy and shows why precise readings matter: a rotating Earth is a specific proposal, not automatically modern heliocentrism.
established: Golapada stanza 9 uses a moving-boat analogy for apparent westward stellar motion.
Kalakriya stanza 10 supplies the conventional 499 CE epoch.
limitations: The following stanza has a conflicting-looking account; the inspected translation discusses this textual difficulty.
The text locates Earth centrally and must not be presented as the modern Sun-centred planetary system.

sources.locator: Kalakriya III.10, pp. 54–55; Golapada IV.6 and IV.9–10, pp. 64–67
supports: The dated verse and editor's chronological explanation were inspected alongside the boat analogy and explicit discussion of conflicting adjacent wording.

contextLinks.note: Both texts discuss Earth's motion, but the inspected material does not establish a transmission route between them.

events.title: Ibn al-Haytham investigates light and vision
events.summary: In the Book of Optics, Ibn al-Haytham examined competing explanations of vision and argued that light and colour from visible objects affect the eye. His investigation combines geometrical reasoning with controlled arrangements and repeated inspection. The opening methodological discussion treats investigators as fallible and calls for criticism of assumptions as well as careful observation.
events.significance: The work connects theories of perception to inspectable procedures, adding an Arabic scientific tradition to the chronology without reducing a cumulative history to one inventor.
established: Book I examines whether vision depends on something coming from objects to the eye.
The work describes controlled viewing arrangements and an explicitly critical investigative procedure.
limitations: The entry does not claim that Ibn al-Haytham invented experimentation or the scientific method.
Only the specified direct-vision passages are assessed; this is not a validation of the whole historical optical system.

sources.locator: Book I, chapters 1–2, printed pp. 3–7; chapter 6, pp. 76–79
supports: The opening sets out rival vision theories and a critical method; chapter 6 argues that visible forms of light and colour produce effects in the eye.

events.title: Shen Kuo records magnetic-needle behaviour
events.summary: In Dream Pool Essays, Shen Kuo describes magnetised needles that tend to point south while deviating slightly eastward. He compares ways of supporting them, including water, a fingernail, a bowl edge and fine silk. The passage records practical observation and technique, and ends by acknowledging that he cannot explain the underlying reason for the behaviour.
events.significance: A precise account of an ordinary instrument reveals how useful knowledge can advance through comparison and admitted uncertainty, without requiring a complete theory of magnetism.
established: The passage describes a small deviation from due south.
It compares support methods and notes that some magnetised needles point north.
limitations: This is not a claim that Shen Kuo invented the compass or discovered every aspect of magnetic declination.
The work's compilation date does not date each reported observation precisely.

events.title: Al-Tusi reworks mathematical astronomy
events.summary: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's Memoir on Astronomy reconsidered the mathematical system associated with Ptolemy. A surviving Arabic manuscript preserves diagrams, including one identified by its custodians as the Tusi couple, a construction connecting circular and linear motion. The manuscript record makes this work traceable while distinguishing its thirteenth-century composition from the later date of the surviving copy.
events.significance: The manuscript places mathematical model building in a wider scholarly geography and preserves a concrete contribution without assuming that every later resemblance proves direct borrowing.
established: The custodial catalog dates the work's composition after 1256.
British Library Or 11209 contains a diagram catalogued as the Tusi couple at folio 32v.
limitations: The Arabic treatise was not fully translated or mathematically reconstructed in this review; the diagram's identification follows its custodial catalog.
The inspected sources do not establish a transmission path to Copernicus.

events.title: Gutenberg's workshop prints the Latin Bible
events.summary: In Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg and his associates produced the large-format Latin Bible now associated with his name. Printing made numerous closely matching texts available, but the books still needed hand-finishing by rubricators, illuminators and binders. Surviving copies therefore record both a new production process and the continued work of manuscript-era craftspeople.
events.significance: The milestone concerns the reproducibility and circulation of texts, a practical condition for comparing claims and building shared knowledge across readers separated by distance.
established: The Library of Congress dates production in Mainz to 1454–1455.
Printed copies were subsequently finished by hand and differ in their decoration and binding.
limitations: This is a European Bible-production milestone, not the beginning of printing worldwide.
The exact distribution of work among all workshop staff and later artisans is not recoverable from this guide.

events.title: Copernicus publishes a Sun-centred planetary system
events.summary: De revolutionibus placed Earth among the planets moving around the Sun and explained the daily appearance of the heavens through Earth's rotation. Copernicus presented a mathematical reordering of an inherited astronomical problem. Its publication also depended on Rheticus carrying the project forward and Johannes Petreius's Nuremberg press, while an anonymous preface complicated how readers encountered the argument.
events.significance: The book changed the arrangement under discussion and made it available for calculation and criticism; publishing a model and establishing all its claims remained different tasks.
established: Book I, chapter 10, places the Sun centrally and Earth among the revolving planets.
The 1543 Nuremberg printing was produced by Petreius after Rheticus helped bring the manuscript to publication.
limitations: The book's historical planetary model should not be equated in every detail with current astronomy.
Osiander's anonymous prefatory account of hypotheses is distinct from Copernicus's own text.

supports: The primary chapter arranges the planets around the Sun, includes Earth's annual orbit and describes the associated apparent planetary motions.

events.title: Kepler publishes a revised orbit for Mars
events.summary: In Astronomia nova, Johannes Kepler used Tycho Brahe's observations of Mars to test and revise planetary models. The resulting account replaced a circular orbit for Mars with an ellipse and addressed changing orbital speed. The published work preserves an extended process of mathematical trial and correction, rather than a single observation that immediately revealed the answer.
events.significance: The episode connects better observations with willingness to revise a preferred geometry, while preserving the separate contributions of the observer and the mathematical investigator.
established: The first edition was published in 1609.
A primary diagram in chapter 59 depicts an ellipse; the custodial history identifies it with the revised Mars orbit.
limitations: The third planetary law belongs to Kepler's later work, not this 1609 publication.
This review inspected a primary diagram and custodial account, not the complete Latin calculations or a numerical replication.

events.title: Galileo publishes telescopic observations
events.summary: Sidereus nuncius reported observations made with Galileo's improved telescope: an uneven lunar surface, numerous previously unseen stars and changing points of light near Jupiter. Repeated observations led him to identify four bodies orbiting that planet. The book also acknowledges news of a telescope made elsewhere, placing his observations within a developing craft of optical instruments.
events.significance: The publication made new observations available for checking and debate, while showing that instruments extend perception through an interaction of manufacture, repeated use and interpretation.
established: The narrative records changing configurations near Jupiter across successive January observations.
The 1610 text describes lunar unevenness and additional stars revealed by the telescope.
limitations: These observations did not by themselves establish every part of a Sun-centred cosmology.
Galileo's later observations of Venus's phases are not imported into this publication.

contextLinks.note: Both entries concern the arrangement of celestial motions; the Jupiter observations alone are not labelled a complete proof of Copernicus's system.

events.title: Descartes publishes his Discourse on Method
events.summary: In Discourse on Method, René Descartes described a personal programme for directing inquiry. Its four precepts call for careful assent, dividing difficulties, moving in order from simpler matters to more complex ones, and checking completeness. The work presents a proposed discipline of reasoning within a wider philosophical project, rather than a neutral manual already shared by all investigators.
events.significance: The entry makes methods themselves part of the history of inquiry: rules for judging claims can be proposed, scrutinised and revised alongside claims about nature.
established: Part II states four precepts governing inquiry and review.
The first edition was printed by Jan Maire in Leiden in 1637.
limitations: This publication did not originate all systematic reasoning or experimental practice.
Descartes's wider metaphysical arguments are not treated as experimentally established findings.

sources.locator: Parts I–II, especially Part II's four precepts
supports: Descartes introduces the route of his own thinking and sets out four procedures for accepting, dividing, ordering and reviewing problems.

events.title: Newton publishes the Principia
events.summary: Newton's Principia set out laws of motion and a mathematical treatment of gravitational attraction, connecting terrestrial and celestial problems within one framework. Its arguments developed relationships between quantities of matter, changes of motion and forces. Edmond Halley's encouragement helped bring the work into print, while Newton continued revising the book after its first edition.
events.significance: The book made a broad range of motions answerable to shared mathematical arguments, illustrating the explanatory reach of a model without making its historical form final.
established: The first edition states three laws of motion.
Book III, proposition VII, presents gravity as proportional to quantity of matter.
limitations: Later additions, including the General Scholium, must not be dated to the 1687 first edition.
A mathematical account of gravitational attraction is distinct from an explanation of its underlying physical mechanism.

events.title: Faraday demonstrates electromagnetic induction
events.summary: Using an iron ring wound with separate coils, Michael Faraday found that changing the current in one circuit produced a brief electrical effect in the other. His subsequent report compared arrangements involving coils and magnets. The important feature was change: establishing or interrupting a magnetic condition could induce a current without a direct electrical connection between the circuits.
events.significance: The experiment made a new relationship between electricity and magnetism measurable, with apparatus and repeatable changes connecting an observed effect to later mathematical accounts.
established: The preserved ring apparatus is associated with the experiment of 29 August 1831.
The primary report distinguishes brief induced effects from the absence of a sustained effect under unchanged conditions.
limitations: The date marks one documented experiment within a continuing programme of investigation.
The effect depends on changing conditions; the experiment does not describe a permanent current from an unchanging arrangement.

supports: Faraday reports transient induced effects and reversals when experimental magnetic conditions change.

events.title: Darwin and Wallace's selection papers are presented
events.summary: The Linnean Society received a joint communication containing Charles Darwin's earlier writings and Alfred Russel Wallace's independently developed essay on species change. Charles Lyell and Joseph Dalton Hooker arranged its presentation. The texts proposed that differences affecting survival and reproduction could preserve some variants over others, offering a natural process through which populations could change over generations.
events.significance: The episode joins a powerful biological explanation to a visible record of overlapping discovery, reminding readers that scientific credit and communication are part of knowledge production.
established: The communication was read on 1 July 1858 and published on 20 August.
Lyell and Hooker's covering text describes independently developed arguments by Darwin and Wallace.
limitations: These writings do not supply the later genetic account of inheritance.
Natural selection is not a ladder of inevitable progress or an explanation of the first origin of life.

events.title: Maxwell publishes an electromagnetic theory of light
events.summary: Maxwell's A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field described interacting electrical and magnetic processes and derived a wave account of light. He compared the calculated propagation speed with independent electrical measurements and measurements of light's speed. The argument explicitly built on experimental work, including Faraday's, while expressing parts of its explanation through the mechanical-medium ideas of its period.
events.significance: The paper linked apparently different phenomena through a quantitative theory, showing how agreement between independent measurements can strengthen an explanation while its conceptual machinery continues to change.
established: Part VI compares electromagnetic propagation with measured light speed and identifies light as an electromagnetic disturbance.
The paper explicitly discusses Faraday's experiments and induction.
limitations: The paper's mechanical-medium assumptions belong to its historical formulation and should not be silently presented as current requirements.
The publication is a theoretical account, not the later experimental production and detection of radio waves.

sources.locator: Part I, sections 1–12, especially 8–9
supports: Maxwell introduces the field account, discusses a mechanical medium and explicitly refers to Faraday and induction.

sources.locator: Part VI, sections 91–97
supports: The paper develops transverse-wave equations, compares electrical and optical measurements and concludes that light is an electromagnetic disturbance.

events.title: Tesla patents a motor driven by alternating currents
events.summary: Nikola Tesla received a US patent for an electromagnetic motor whose separate circuits carry alternating currents timed to shift its magnetic field. The specification describes a motor and generator system designed to produce rotation without a motor commutator. It records a concrete electrical invention within the broader development of alternating current power.
events.significance: A dated patent makes Tesla’s engineering contribution inspectable through a specific mechanism, connecting electrical theory with practical machinery and transmission of mechanical power.
established: US patent 381,968 names Tesla and carries the grant date May 1, 1888.
The specification describes coordinated alternating currents producing a progressively shifting magnetic field.
limitations: A patent documents this claimed invention; it does not establish that Tesla alone invented alternating current technology.
The patent contains no evidence of exotic energy sources or later claims about secret technologies.

events.title: Phoenix Lights — moving formations and a later flare display
events.summary: Arizona witnesses reported moving lights during the evening of March 13, followed around 10 p.m. by a separate row of lights southwest of Phoenix. Accounts differed about whether the earlier lights formed one solid object. Contemporary telescope testimony supported aircraft; military flare drops and later analyses explain the widely recorded later display.
events.significance: A landmark public controversy shows why a memorable case name can conceal different observations. Explanations need to match the particular time, location and evidence.
established: NUFORC’s preliminary 1997 compilation records moving-formation reports across Arizona and cautions that its account preceded written submissions.
In June 1997, Tony Ortega reported that amateur astronomer Mitch Stanley resolved separate aircraft through a telescope. This is a reported visual observation, not a preserved telescope image.
Ortega’s 1998 investigation separately reports military confirmation of a roughly 10 p.m. flare drop. It quotes a Maryland spokesman saying those aircraft did not fly north of Phoenix.
McGaha and Nickell’s 2015 assessment argues for aircraft in the earlier formation and describes McGaha’s interview with the later flare-flight leader. Portions repeat the earlier reporting.
limitations: Neither the later flare explanation nor the aircraft account establishes the identity of every reported light. No calibrated raw imagery, complete flight logs or independent reconstruction was inspected here.
Witness recollections differ in perceived size, height and solidity. Unresolved details do not establish a non-human craft.
A 2026 internet-questionnaire paper concerns respondents’ remembered experiences and attitudes. Only its abstract was inspected; it does not supply a physical identification.
openQuestions: Which contemporaneous flight and observation records can securely match the earlier reports to particular aircraft?

events.title: The Dresden Codex preserves Maya astronomy and calculation
events.summary: Maya scribes recorded number tables, calendars and rituals in folding books. The surviving Dresden Codex includes Venus cycles and eclipse tables. It shows careful observation and calculation used within religious life. The book preserves older knowledge; it does not date when that knowledge began.
events.significance: This surviving manuscript lets us study both mathematical skill and the purposes it served.
established: SLUB dates this copy to roughly 1300–1521 in Yucatán. Venus and eclipse tables have specific surviving page locations.
Maya calendars combine 260-day, 365-day and longer counts; their number system uses place value and a zero concept.
limitations: Only a few codices survive. Their tables cannot stand for every Maya community or period. Long Count creation dates are mythic anchors.
tags: Yucatán peninsula, Mexico; manuscript now in Dresden, Germany

events.title: The Popol Vuh survives through a K’iche’ text and translation
events.summary: The Popol Vuh tells K’iche’ Maya stories of creation, the Hero Twins and the underworld, as well as community history. The best-known surviving manuscript pairs K’iche’ with Spanish. Francisco Ximénez copied it in Guatemala around 1700–1715, drawing on an earlier Indigenous text.
events.significance: It preserves a specific community’s sacred history through a colonial-era chain of transmission.
established: Newberry identifies the manuscript, its two languages and approximate copying period.
limitations: The earlier sixteenth-century text is not the same as the surviving copy. Translation and colonial conditions shape what we can recover; stories are not dated physical events.

limitations: This range selects milestones; earlier work and continuing Maya-language scholarship also matter. Not every glyph or ancient passage is resolved.

events.summary: December 21, 2012 marked a major Long Count cycle boundary. It did not end Maya culture or demonstrate a prediction that the world would end. Contemporary Maya voices, calendar practice and modern disaster stories belong to different parts of this history.

established: NMAI’s calendar guide identifies the cycle date and continuing calendar practice; period reporting separates it from apocalypse claims.
limitations: Maya communities hold diverse views. The portal’s linked interviews were not watched, and no single view is attributed to all Maya people.

events.title: Tenochtitlan’s water systems support a great city
events.summary: The Mexica capital expanded on land reclaimed from Lake Texcoco. Canals carried people and goods. Raised causeways linked the city to the shore, and aqueducts brought fresh water. Much of its building took place from the 1470s until the 1521 conquest.
events.significance: Engineering made urban life possible, while tribute and imperial power helped pay for it.
established: The Met documents reclaimed land, canals, three causeways and two aqueducts.
limitations: This is a major building phase, not a precise founding date. Urban achievements do not erase coercion, war or the different experiences of subject peoples.

events.title: Acre earthworks reveal a long history of forest management
events.summary: Researchers studied soil and plant traces around ancient earthworks in Acre, Brazil. Their results suggest that people managed useful trees and cleared selected areas over long periods. The forest was neither untouched nor uniformly cleared.

limitations: These sites do not represent every Amazonian landscape. Ancient forest management is not equivalent to the scale or effects of modern deforestation.

events.title: People develop farming in several regions
events.dateNotes: Rounded navigation bounds for the early and middle Holocene periods highlighted by Larson and colleagues: 12,000–4,000 calendar years BP, explicitly relative to 1950. Not one invention date or the end of agricultural innovation.
events.summary: Cultivation, domestication and farming developed gradually and independently in multiple regions, including parts of Asia, Africa, Oceania and the Americas. Communities worked with different plants and animals; growing food and fully domesticating a species were different steps.
events.significance: Food production helped sustain denser settlements and larger populations while reshaping landscapes. It also brought disease risks and habitat loss; it was not an uncomplicated improvement for everyone.
established: Archaeological and genetic syntheses support multiple independent centers and processes lasting centuries or millennia.
Cultivation can precede the biological traits used to identify domestication.
limitations: Regional chronologies differ. Farming, herding, gathering and hunting often coexisted; the broad range does not describe every community.

items.reason: A mathematical theory unified electromagnetic phenomena and light, a major explanatory connection rather than the creation of every later application.
items.question: What becomes possible when phenomena once studied separately fit one explanation?

items.reason: Microscopy supported distinct neuronal structures, a concrete contribution to understanding nervous tissue rather than a full explanation of consciousness.

items.reason: Patented alternating-current motor arrangements gave a practical electrical-machine contribution; industrial electrification cannot be attributed to this patent alone.
items.question: Why does an invention need systems, workers and investment to become widely useful?

items.reason: An account of the stream of thought made a lasting psychological question explicit; introspective description is distinct from a complete neural mechanism.

items.reason: Demonstrates that democratic participation was fought for and could still exclude people.
items.question: Who can vote, who can govern, and which exclusions remain?

items.reason: Evidence for radium extended knowledge of radioactive matter; the announcement did not itself establish all later medical uses or their risks.
items.question: How can evidence of a new material open questions about both benefits and risks?

items.reason: Finite energy elements supplied a crucial step in radiation theory and quantum development; later quantum mechanics was a separate achievement.
items.question: When can a successful calculation point toward a new physical idea?

items.reason: Controlled powered flights demonstrated a technical capability through recorded tests; aircraft diffusion depended on later collective work.
items.question: What must be controlled to turn a flight attempt into a repeatable capability?

items.reason: Special relativity reformulated space, time and motion for a specified physical domain, changing rather than abolishing older useful approximations.
items.question: Which familiar assumptions about time and space depend on how we move?

items.reason: Scattering analysis replaced a diffuse atomic model with a concentrated center, a substantial experimentally bounded structural inference.
items.question: How can patterns of scattering reveal structures too small to see directly?

items.reason: A relation between variable-star periods and brightness supplied an astronomical distance tool, with calibration and later uses distinct from this initial work.
items.question: How can one measured relationship become a tool for measuring distance?

items.reason: Explains a major break in the international order and the human costs behind it.
items.question: How do war, its settlement and later political choices interact?

items.reason: Field equations changed gravitation into a geometrical theory with testable consequences; later confirmations do not belong to the submission date.
items.question: What observations could test a different explanation of gravity?

items.reason: Cepheid distances placed spiral nebulae beyond the Milky Way, transforming the demonstrated scale of the astronomical world.
items.question: How did measuring distance change the scale of the known universe?

items.reason: Atomic analysis of stellar atmospheres changed the interpretation of stellar composition; collaboration and the broader spectral program remain part of the story.
items.question: How do measurements of light tell us what distant stars contain?

items.reason: A wave equation supplied a predictive mathematical framework for atomic energy levels, within a wider collective quantum-mechanics development.
items.question: What does a mathematical prediction tell us, and what does it leave open?

items.reason: A model connected expansion with measured redshifts; cosmological inference remained dependent on later measurements and alternatives.
items.question: How do mathematical models and measurements of galaxies constrain each other?

items.reason: Makes systematic persecution and its lasting human consequences visible in shared history.
items.question: How can discrimination become organized violence, and what responsibilities do others have?

items.reason: Radio detection of an aircraft demonstrated a practical sensing capability; mature radar systems required subsequent engineering.
items.question: How can reflected signals extend what people can detect?

items.reason: Formalizing computation exposed what specified machines can calculate and where limits arise; this paper did not itself build modern computers.
items.question: Are there limits to what a perfectly specified procedure can calculate?

items.reason: Explaining uranium splitting clarified a mechanism essential to nuclear energy and weapons, without collapsing discovery, reactor operation and weapon deployment.
items.question: How can the same physical mechanism support energy production and destruction?

items.reason: A specific advocacy letter urged state attention to nuclear research; it explains a documented policy intervention without making Einstein a bomb designer.
items.question: When can scientific knowledge become a responsibility to inform public decisions?

items.reason: The modern manuscript discovery expanded the accessible evidence for early religious diversity; it did not create the ancient beliefs it reveals.
items.question: How can recovering old documents change the questions historians can ask?

items.question: What changes when a destructive capability moves from theory to demonstration?

items.question: How should a society govern a technology with civilian and military uses?

items.question: How do new institutions change the way a government makes and checks decisions?

items.question: How can a channel carry information reliably despite noise?

items.reason: Explains a central language of modern rights and why implementation still matters.
items.question: What turns a declaration of rights into practical protection?

items.reason: Decipherment recovered historical names and dynastic records through multiple researchers' work, changing what surviving inscriptions could establish.
items.question: What changes when images can be read as names, words and histories?

items.reason: A structure tied to experimental evidence explained DNA organization, providing a major molecular-biological account with collective credit and subsequent questions.
items.question: How did structure, measurements and collective work change our understanding of heredity?

items.question: How did a small satellite change what governments chose to build?

items.reason: An advanced defense-research agency created a durable organizational vehicle for technical projects, without validating speculative technologies attributed to it.
items.question: What does organizing and funding research establish, and what does it not?

items.question: How can an institution turn an ambition into a continuing research program?

items.question: Whose essential work can disappear behind a celebrated mission?

items.reason: A mathematical inequality made a class of local models experimentally testable; later violations are separate records and do not imply mind-powered communication.
items.question: How can a disagreement about reality become an experimentally testable question?

items.question: What traces could distinguish different histories of the universe?

items.reason: Resolving regular pulses uncovered a new astronomical phenomenon through anomaly checks and collective observing work.
items.question: How do repeated checks turn a strange signal into a scientific finding?

items.question: What systems and collective labor make a difficult mission possible?

items.reason: Galaxy rotation measurements strengthened a mass-distribution problem with instrument-enabled evidence, leaving the physical explanation open.

items.reason: Shows how scientific evidence and uncertainty can inform action involving many governments.
items.question: How can governments act on strong evidence while remaining honest about uncertainty?

reviewExceptions: Blombos, Katherine Johnson and recovered Indigenous texts reveal larger histories without being credited as the sole cause of them.
Separate modern confirmations, instrument-image releases, administrative effective dates and repeating disclosure editions stay in full history, where related records remain linked.
No UFO/disclosure record is selected merely to maintain its former numerical share. NASA methods, consciousness and encounter material remain accessible through their explicit views and topics.
